chunks: Al-ʿAmrakī narrated from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليهما السلام, who said:

I asked him about a chicken, a pigeon, and the like that step on filth and then enter the water: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it for salat (prayer)? He said: “No, unless the water is abundant, in the measure of a kurr of water.”
And I asked him about the lizard, the snake, and the gecko falling into water without dying in it: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it for salat (prayer)? He said: “There is no harm in it.”
And I asked him about a mouse that fell into a jar of oil, then was taken out before it died: may he sell it to a Muslim? He said: “Yes, and he may apply it as oil.”
And this report does not contradict.

key_terms.الْعَذِرَةَ: filth or fecal impurity stepped on by the animal
key_terms.الْمَاءِ: water being assessed for use in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الْوَزَغِ: the gecko mentioned among creatures falling into water
key_terms.حُبِّ دُهْنٍ: a jar or container of oil
key_terms.فَأْرَةٍ: a mouse that fell into the oil
key_terms.كُرٍّ: the legal measure of abundant water that is not easily affected
key_terms.يَدَّهِنُ: to anoint or apply as oil
key_terms.يُتَوَضَّأُ: to perform wudu (ablution) with that water

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings on water or oil touched by animals or impurity according to this hadith from Tahdhib al-Ahkam?
ai.summary: This hadith presents legal rulings on taharah and the use of water and oil after contact with animals or impurity. It distinguishes between cases affecting the validity of wudu (ablution), including the rule of abundant water reaching the measure of kurr, and also addresses permissibility in a commercial context.
